purpose: Adds a version-tracked upgrade routine (new wppo_version option) that runs a full wp_cache_flush() on plugin activation/update to evict legacy WP 6.9 pre-salt query-group cache keys left behind by the plugin's Redis object-cache drop-in (issue #489).
riskRationale: The eviction logic is technically sound and verified against the drop-in's key layout, but the migration re-fires a full object-cache flush on every future version bump and on fresh activation (cache-stampede risk), a failed flush is silently marked complete so the eviction never retries, and the commit bulk-commits ~4,700 dev-only Composer files (~525K lines) into the production-tracked vendor/ tree, some of which would ship in the release ZIP.
breakingChanges: Every plugin version change and fresh activation now triggers a full object-cache flush (cold-cache rebuild / stampede window on Redis-backed sites)
git-tracked vendor/ grows by ~4,700 dev-only files (~525K lines); phpunit/mockery/patchwork/wpcs packages are not excluded by .distignore and risk shipping in the WordPress.org ZIP

text: The migration approach is well-reasoned and verified: because the drop-in builds group patterns as {blog_prefix}{salt}{group}:* (templates/object-cache.php get_key()), flush_group() misses the legacy unsalted keys while flush()'s SCAN of {blog_prefix}* covers both, so a full wp_cache_flush() is the only reliable eviction. The version-tracked routine with a manage_options guard and cheap early-exit is a clean skeleton. However, the routine is not actually one-time (it re-flushes on every future release and on fresh installs), discards the flush result so failures are never retried, and the commit accidentally bundles the entire dev Composer toolchain into the tracked vendor/ directory. Needs cleanup before merge.

reasoning: The core eviction logic is correct, but the migration must be gated to run exactly once (dedicated sentinel or version floor), must only persist the version when the flush succeeds, and vendor/ must be rebuilt production-only via `composer release` before committing. All three blockers are small, mechanical fixes with no regression risk.

message: The technical analysis is correct and verified against the drop-in: flush_group() builds its pattern via get_key('', $group) as {blog_prefix}{salt}{group}:* (templates/object-cache.php:573), which misses legacy unsalted keys, while flush() SCANs {blog_prefix}* (templates/object-cache.php:527) and covers both salted and unsalted keys — so a full wp_cache_flush() with a function_exists() guard is genuinely the right, minimal mechanism.

Clean version-tracked upgrade skeleton: a single cheap option read with early exit once versions match, version persisted with autoload=false (no autoload bloat), and correct hook ordering in Activate::init() so the activity-log table exists before Log::add() runs.

The admin_init wiring mirrors the existing maybe_fix_wp_cache() pattern and is guarded by current_user_can('manage_options'), so only privileged users can trigger the flush on the routine-update path that never fires register_activation_hook.

The migration is not actually one-time: it only checks WPPO_VERSION === $stored_version, so every future plugin release (1.8.2, 1.9.0, ...) — even JS-only or cosmetic bumps — re-runs a full wp_cache_flush() on the first admin visit, purging the entire object cache (transients, other plugins' cached data, object-cache-backed sessions) and recreating the stampede risk this issue is meant to prevent. The legacy unsalted keys can only exist once (the flush evicts them), so re-flushing on later updates has no benefit.
suggestion: Gate the flush behind a dedicated one-time sentinel option, or scope it to a fixed version floor equal to the release that first ships this fix (e.g. stored_version < 1.8.1), independently of the version-roll-forward gate used for future migrations.

message: The boolean return value of Cache::flush_legacy_query_cache_keys() is discarded and wppo_version is persisted unconditionally, so a failed flush (e.g. Redis momentarily down — the drop-in's flush() returns true even when disconnected, merely clearing the in-memory array) permanently marks the migration complete and the stale pre-salt keys are never retried, silently defeating the fix's purpose. The log entry claims success regardless of outcome.
suggestion: Only persist the version (and log success) when the flush actually ran; otherwise log a retryable failure and leave the option stale so the eviction runs again on the next admin visit.

message: The commit adds ~4,700 files (~525K insertions) of dev-only Composer packages (phpunit, mockery, brain/monkey, antecedent/patchwork, nikic/php-parser, sebastian/*, squizlabs/php_codesniffer, wp-coding-standards/wpcs, phpcompatibility, phpcsstandards, etc.) to the git-tracked vendor/ directory, growing it from 236 to ~4,967 files. AGENTS.md explicitly requires committing production-only vendor via `composer release` (composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader), and .distignore does NOT exclude most of these newly added packages — so phpunit and friends would be packaged into the WordPress.org release ZIP. The PR's Files Changed list also underreports this (lists only composer metadata).
suggestion: Run `composer release` (composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader) and re-commit only the production vendor tree (voku/html-min, matthiasmullie/minify, woocommerce/action-scheduler); as a belt-and-braces measure, add the dev-only packages to .distignore.

message: On fresh activation/reactivation the stored version option is absent, so the routine runs a full wp_cache_flush() (pointlessly evicting the shared backend on new installs where no legacy keys can exist) and writes a misleading 'Plugin upgraded — legacy cache keys flushed.' activity-log entry even though nothing was upgraded or evicted.
suggestion: Treat an empty stored version as a fresh install: record the version and return without flushing or logging; reserve the flush and log entry for genuine upgrades.

message: WPPO_VERSION is still '1.8.0' while all new code is documented @since 1.8.1. WordPress.org will not deliver this fix to existing 1.8.0 users without a higher version number, and if the release tooling bumps the version later, users who already ran the flush at 1.8.0 will be flushed a second time. The doc annotations and the version constant must agree.
suggestion: Bump the plugin header Version and WPPO_VERSION to 1.8.1 in this PR (or align the @since tags to the actual released version) so the version-gated migration corresponds to a real version boundary.

message: The eviction only fires on admin_init (an admin page view). Sites updated via WP-CLI, WordPress background auto-updates, or managed-hosting pipelines never trigger it, so the legacy #489 keys persist indefinitely for exactly the sites where the bug reproduces. admin_init is acceptable as a convenience path, but a correctness-critical eviction needs a more reliable trigger.
suggestion: Also register the routine on a trigger that fires without an admin visit — e.g. the upgrader_process_complete (or *_after_plugin_updated) hook, a low-frequency WP-Cron event, or an Action Scheduler job — while keeping the manage_options guard for the synchronous admin path.

message: The docblock claims the method is a 'No-op on cores without object caching', but wp_cache_flush() has existed since WP 2.5 and always flushes the in-memory WP_Object_Cache; it is only a no-op with respect to persistent backends. The wording is misleading.
suggestion: Reword to something like 'On cores without a persistent object cache this only flushes the in-memory cache and is harmless.'

message: The new wppo_version option is not added to uninstall.php's delete_option() cleanup list. If a user deactivates/uninstalls (keeping a shared Redis backend) and later reinstalls, the stale 'migration already run' marker suppresses the eviction on the fresh install.
suggestion: Add delete_option( 'wppo_version' ); to uninstall.php alongside the other plugin options.

message: The full flush is unconditional across WordPress versions and cache backends: on WP < 6.9 the pre-salt key problem cannot exist, yet the whole object cache is still evicted on each update, and on any non-WPPO drop-in (Redis Object Cache plugin, Memcached, WP Redis) or a shared multisite backend wp_cache_flush() is global and evicts all sites'/plugins' cached data.
suggestion: Consider gating the flush on WP 6.9+ (e.g. function_exists('wp_cache_add_salt') or version_compare( get_bloginfo('version'), '6.9', '>=' )) and/or on the plugin's own drop-in being active, and document the cross-site blast radius for shared-backend multisite operators.
